subject: Observability benchmark
summary:
Checkout slowed down because the **order-service's database** became severely degraded. The order-service is the main bottleneck in the checkout path.

**What slowed down:** POST /api/orders (checkout) end-to-end latency rose from a baseline of ~30 ms to a p99 of **10 seconds**, with the worst traces reaching 17.6 s. The degradation was concentrated between **~05:03 and ~05:51 UTC on 2026-10-29**.

**Why:** The order-service's database layer suffered escalating slow queries and connection timeouts. Logs show "slow database query" warnings (tables: sessions, orders, products — up to 2,575 ms) and "database connection timeout" errors throughout the window, intensifying during the peak. The database could not serve queries fast enough, causing the order-service to stall on each request.

**Which piece of the stack was the main bottleneck:** The **order-service → database** hop. Traces prove it: in the 17.6 s representative trace, the order-service span consumed 12.7 s while the api-gateway added only ~1.6 s of overhead. In a trace that also called payment-service, that call took only 25 ms (though it errored). Payment-service had its own intermittent errors but its average latency remained 20–50 ms.

**Representative trace ID:** `4715b7764646608b1a48f1b3a2cec04b` (17.6 s POST /api/orders; order-service span = 12.7 s).

impact.summary: Checkout (POST /api/orders) end-to-end latency rose from ~30 ms baseline to p99 of 10 seconds between 05:03–05:51 UTC on 2026-10-29, with individual traces reaching 17.6 s. Order-service average latency peaked at ~5.4 s. During this window, order-service returned 500/502/503 errors on checkout and cart requests, making checkout effectively unusable for customers for roughly 50 minutes.

findings.statement: The order-service's database layer was the root cause of checkout slowness. Logs show 'slow database query' warnings (up to 2,575 ms on sessions, orders, products tables) and 'database connection timeout' errors escalating through the window, peaking during 05:00–05:51 UTC on Oct 29.
findings.mechanism: Database slow queries and connection timeouts caused the order-service to stall on every checkout request, as it must query the database to create/process orders. The database degradation escalated from intermittent slow queries (hundreds of ms) to severe stalls (seconds to tens of seconds), directly inflating checkout latency.

findings.statement: Order-service p99 latency hit 10 seconds and average latency peaked at ~5.4 s during the 05:00–05:51 UTC window on Oct 29, compared to a baseline of ~30–50 ms.
findings.mechanism: The p99 latency histogram for order-service shows the quantile hitting the 10-second bucket (histogram ceiling) for most of the 05:03–05:51 window, meaning at least 1% of requests took ≥10 s. Average latency corroborates, peaking at ~5.4 s around 05:46 UTC.

findings.statement: Traces confirm order-service is the dominant bottleneck. In the 17.6 s representative trace, the order-service span consumed 12.7 s while downstream calls to payment-service took only 25 ms (though that call errored).
findings.mechanism: In trace 4715b7764646608b1a48f1b3a2cec04b, the order-service span (12.7 s) accounted for 72% of the total 17.6 s end-to-end time. The api-gateway added 1.6 s, and the webapp added the remainder. No payment-service span existed in this trace.

findings.statement: Order-service returned a burst of 5xx errors during the peak slowdown (05:00–05:51 UTC), including HTTP 500, 502, and 503 statuses on POST /api/orders and GET /api/cart endpoints.
findings.mechanism: Logs show 9 error entries in just the 05:00–06:00 window, with statuses 500/502/503 and messages like 'request failed', 'internal server error', and 'upstream service error'. A 'retry attempt 3' log at 05:25 indicates the service was retrying failing upstream calls.

findings.statement: Payment-service had intermittent errors (database connection timeouts, upstream service errors) but its average latency remained 20–50 ms with only occasional spikes (~0.7 s). It was a minor contributor to checkout failures but not to checkout latency.
findings.mechanism: Payment-service errors (502/503 on POST /api/payments) meant that even when the order-service could process its part, the payment step could fail. However, the payment-service calls were fast (~20–50 ms), so they did not contribute to latency — only to error rates on traces that included a payment step.

findings.statement: Database issues were not limited to one table — slow queries and connection timeouts affected sessions, orders, products, and users tables, suggesting a systemic database degradation rather than a single problematic query.
findings.mechanism: Slow query logs appeared on sessions (1,214–2,511 ms), orders (613–2,575 ms), products (569–1,028 ms), and users (1,647 ms) tables, indicating a broad database performance issue rather than a single hot query.

hypotheses.statement: The database degradation may have been caused by a missing index, lock contention, or resource exhaustion (CPU/memory) on the database server, but no database-server-level metrics are available to confirm.
hypotheses.test: Query database server metrics (CPU, memory, active connections, lock waits) or examine slow query logs on the database side to identify the specific query or resource bottleneck.

actions.title: Investigate the order-service database server
actions.rationale: The order-service database is the confirmed bottleneck. Investigating database server health (CPU, memory, disk I/O, connection pool saturation, lock contention) will identify the underlying cause of the slow queries and timeouts.
actions.verification: Database server metrics show the resource bottleneck (e.g., CPU saturation, lock waits, connection pool exhaustion).

actions.title: Add circuit breaker / timeout for order-service database calls
actions.rationale: The checkout flow has no circuit breaker around the order-service database. When the database stalls, the entire checkout path blocks. A timeout + circuit breaker would fail fast and allow partial degradation instead of full stalls.
actions.verification: Order-service returns 503 quickly under database degradation instead of stalling for 10+ seconds.

actions.title: Review and add database indexes for frequently queried tables
actions.rationale: Slow queries on sessions, orders, products, and users tables suggest missing or stale indexes. Adding appropriate indexes or tuning queries can prevent recurrence.
actions.verification: Query execution plans show index usage; slow query warnings decrease in frequency.

actions.title: Check if order-service and payment-service share a database instance
actions.rationale: The payment-service also logged 'database connection timeout' errors. Both services may share the same database or connection pool. Separating them or increasing pool size could reduce cross-service impact.
actions.verification: Infrastructure review confirms whether they share a database; if so, isolation or pool resizing reduces contention.

limitations.statement: No database-server-level metrics (CPU, memory, disk, connection pool, lock waits) are available in Prometheus. The root cause can only be traced to the database layer, not to the specific database-internal mechanism.

Tempo trace search for a 'checkout' service returned empty — there is no dedicated checkout service; the checkout flow spans order-service, payment-service, api-gateway, and webapp. Initial service label guesses were wrong.
Several Loki log queries using compound pipe filters (|= 'slow' or |= 'timeout') were rejected by Loki. Only single-term filters worked, which may have missed some relevant log entries.
